analysis.one_liner: Eases federal black lung benefit rules for disabled coal miners and widows, shifting costs to mine operators.
analysis.headline: The Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee held one hearing in March 1994 but never voted the bill out of committee, and it died when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the federal program that pays monthly benefits to coal miners disabled by black lung disease and to their survivors. Miners who were paid benefits and later denied would no longer have to repay the money unless they had committed fraud, and past repayments would be refunded. It would make it easier for widows to qualify, make winning claimants' legal fees payable by the coal operator, let miners whose claims were denied after 1981 get a fresh review, and extend coverage for the first time to workers at coke ovens. The costs would fall on coal mine operators and on the federal Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, which is financed by a tax on coal.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners disabled by black lung disease, their widows and widowers, and coke oven workers. Disabled miners would keep benefits already paid even if a later ruling went against them, unless fraud was involved, and would get refunds of money they had been forced to repay. Winning claimants would have attorney fees and expert costs paid by the responsible coal operator or the trust fund. Miners whose claims were denied after January 1982 could refile for a fresh review on the merits. Survivors would qualify if married at least nine months or if they had a child with the miner, and widows who remarry after age 50 would keep their benefits. Coke oven workers, whose lung disease was previously outside the program, would be covered.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Disabled coal miners and their widows

how_it_helps.text: Miners finally denied benefits after an initial award would not have to repay the money unless they used fraud or deception, and the trust fund would refund past repayments.
A miner who was receiving benefits for, or totally disabled by, black lung at death would be presumed to have died from the disease, opening survivor benefits.

Winning claimants would be entitled to all reasonable attorney fees and expert costs, paid by the responsible operator or the trust fund, with payment guaranteed within 45 days of the fee determination.
Any claim filed after January 1, 1982 and denied before enactment could be refiled for a completely new review on the merits.

Widows and widowers who remarry after age 50 would keep survivor benefits, and evidence rules would cap medical exams while giving substantial weight to a board-certified treating physician's opinion.
Coke oven workers would be covered by the black lung program and the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act for the first time.

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators designated as responsible operators, who would pay monthly benefits, refunds of claimant repayments, and claimants' attorney and expert fees, and the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, which reimburses operators when no responsible operator exists and is financed by an excise tax on coal. Operators would also face faster payment deadlines and potential cost assessments for contesting liability without reasonable grounds.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal mine operators and the coal tax fund

drawbacks.text: The bill shifts real costs onto coal operators and the trust fund: waived overpayment recoveries, refunds of past repayments, and mandatory payment of claimants' legal fees all add liability the industry and the coal-tax-financed fund would bear.
Allowing any claim denied after January 1982 to be refiled for a fresh review would reopen thousands of closed cases and could add substantial long-term liabilities to the program.

The new survivor rules still leave some families out: widows and widowers married to the miner for less than nine months with no child together, and those who remarry before age 50, would remain disqualified.

The evidence provisions cut both ways: claimants would be limited to three medical exams and one interpretive opinion per party, which an honest supporter would acknowledge narrows the record even as it limits operators' ability to shop for contrary exams.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would clearly help disabled miners and widows, and its costs would fall mainly on the coal industry rather than general taxpayers, since the trust fund is financed by a coal excise tax. The main honest objection is the refile provision: reopening every claim denied since 1982 for a new review is a large retroactive expansion whose fiscal size is hard to bound, and it is what made the bill a significant cost item for operators. The other changes—no repayment absent fraud, treating-physician weight, fee shifting—are conventional pro-claimant fixes to a program long criticized for denying claims on procedural grounds.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which held a hearing in March 1994 but never voted to send it to the Senate floor, and it died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Sen. Paul Simon introduced the bill on November 23, 1993, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
The committee held hearings on March 15, 1994, printed as S.Hrg. 103-514, but took no further action on the bill.
No floor vote, committee vote, or further Senate action ever occurred, and the bill died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators came out ahead: they never faced the expanded benefit liability, refunds of claimant repayments, mandatory attorney-fee payments, and coverage of coke oven workers the bill would have imposed. Disabled miners and widows hoping for relief from repayments and refiled claims got nothing.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no floor division is recorded; the four original sponsors and all seven cosponsors were Democrats, several from coal states, and no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.note: Operators found responsible for a miner's disease would pay benefits promptly, could not claw back overpayments from miners absent fraud, and would cover winning claimants' attorney and expert fees. The bill's whole purpose was to shift claim costs back onto the industry that caused the disease, so operators had every reason to let it sit.

Coke oven workers would be brought under the black lung program and the Mine Safety and Health Act for the first time, creating a new class of claimants and new employer liability. Coke oven workers face heavy respiratory hazards from oven emissions.

industries.industry: Black Lung Disability Trust Fund (coal excise tax)
industries.note: The fund would pay refunds, reimburse operators for overpayments on denied claims, and cover claimants' legal fees where no operator is responsible, but it also gains from waived overpayment recoveries against miners. The fund is financed by a per-ton tax on coal, so its costs fall on the coal industry rather than general taxpayers.
